Abstract
Due to the high reflectance and heat conductivity of copper and its alloys, the processing window for laser-based powder bed 
fusion (PBF-LB/M) processing of high-density copper components fundamentally overlaps with conduction and keyhole 
melting zones, resulting in the emergence of certain pores in the structure of printed parts. The present research aims to study 
how the development of process-induced lack-of-fusion or keyhole porosities during the PBF-LB/M process can affect the 
anisotropic microstructure and mechanical properties of the produced copper alloys. For this purpose, several samples were 
produced utilizing a similar CuCrZr-feedstock composition but varied process parameters from different areas of the PBF-
LB/M processing window, specifically at laser powers of 300 W and 380 W which define the boarders of the conduction and 
keyhole regimes. X-ray computed tomography (XCT) revealed that the 300-W and 380-W samples achieved relative densities 
of 98.88% and 99.99%, respectively, with elongated lack-of-fusion pores forming at 300 W and semi-spherical keyhole pores 
at 380 W. Microstructural analyses employing scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction 
(EBSD) demonstrated strong anisotropy in different build directions of the samples, owing to the growth of long columnar 
grains with intense < 101 > orientation along the build directions. Here, the emergence of different types of pores can cause 
competition between the epitaxial growth of columnar grains and the heterogeneous nucleation of new grains on the layers’ 
interfaces, thereby significantly varying the grain size, preferred orientation, crystallographic texture, and microstructural 
anisotropy of the samples. Furthermore, compression tests and nanoindentation measurements of the printed alloys in the 
longitudinal and transverse directions revealed that the 300 W and 380 W samples exhibited compressive strength anisotropies 
of 0.061 and 0.072, and average nanoindentation hardness values of 1.3 GPa and 1.5 GPa, respectively. The orientation of 
elongated lack-of-fusion porosities perpendicular to the loading axis was identified as the most damaging factor, significantly 
reducing mechanical performance compared to the uniformly distributed keyhole pores.

1  Introduction
Laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M) is one 
of the most common types of additive manufacturing tech-
niques and is widely used for the three-dimensional printing 
of metallic parts like stainless steel, titanium, aluminum, and 
Ni-based superalloys [1, 2]. This process is based on the suc-
cessive fusion and welding of the metal powder using a laser 
beam and offers rapid printing of the near-net-shaped parts 
with low material waste [2, 3]. Respected to these advan-
tages, PBF-LB/M processing of copper-based components 
is highly demanded for the manufacturing of complex elec-
trical and thermally conductive parts. However, PBF-LB/M 
processing of particularly dense and functional copper-based 
components proves challenging due to some specific physi-
cal properties of the copper powder. Here, a central hurdle 
is that copper powder highly reflects the applied laser and 
spreads the generated heat (due to their high reflectivity

and conductivity), so limited powder melting and sintering 
mostly result in the preparation of parts with high porosity

In recent years, several methods based on powder or laser 
development approaches have been evaluated for improving 
copper PBF-LB/M processability. In the powder develop-
ment approach, specific elements are alloyed into copper 
particles or coated on their surfaces to increase the overall 
laser absorption of the powder feedstock [4–7]. For example, 
alloyed CuCrZr powder is a typical precipitation-strength-
ened alloy that, compared with pure copper, provides a much 
higher laser absorption coefficient of 37% [8, 9]. Owing 
to their excellent mechanical strength, high electrical and 
thermal conductivity, good formability, and high creep and 
fatigue resistance, CuCrZr alloys find widespread applica-
tions in aerospace, electronics, and heat-transfer industries, 
including rocket engine heat exchangers, combustion cham-
bers, cooling channels of rocket nozzles, integrated circuit 
lead frames, railway contact wires, and electrodes of resist-
ance welding [8–11]. On the other side, the laser develop-
ment approaches utilize higher-power or lower-wavelength 
lasers (like green and blue) to increase the intensity of the 
irradiated laser beam and facilitate the copper particles melt-
ing [4, 12–15]. In this regard, irradiating highly conductive 
copper powder with a high-power laser significantly affects 
the powder melting and melt-pool solidification mecha-
nisms, which induce a variety of porosities and structural 
defects in the printed parts. Depending on the PBF-LB/M 
processing conditions, three modes of conduction, transi-
tion, and keyhole were introduced to explain the melting 
and pore evaluation in the printed samples [16, 17]. The con-
duction melting mode is mostly observed when lower laser 
energy input is utilized during the PBF-LB/M processing, 
so heat conduction as the dominant heat-transfer mechanism 
is not sufficient to completely melt the tracks, and so-called 
lack-of-fusion pores of highly irregular shapes are formed 
between the tracks. In the keyhole melting mode, in contrast, 
higher PBF-LB/M laser energy input dominates the convec-
tion heat-transfer mechanism and causes deep penetration 
melting, metal evaporation, the collapse of vapor cavities, 
and subsequently inducing small and spherical keyhole pores 
within the tracks [16, 18–20]. In addition, the irregular flow 
of shielding gas over a powder bed can disrupt the melt’s 
pool convective heat transfer and result in the evaluation of 
keyhole porosities [21]. The PBF-LB/M processing of highly 
dense samples is performed in the region between the con-
duction and keyhole modes, named transition mode, where 
the optimal combination of process parameters controls 
the powder melting and melt-pool solidification. However, 
many researchers reported that due to the high conductivity 
of copper and its alloys, the PBF-LB/M process window is 
very narrow, so small variations of the process parameters 
result in a sudden change in melting behavior [19, 20, 22, 
23]. Accordingly, low amounts of keyholes, lack-of-fusion, 
and other types of defects are commonly observed within 
the optimized copper components produced in the transi-
tion regions.
Aside from the porosity development, different PBF-
LB/M modes and processing conditions can greatly affect 
the microstructural features and properties of the printed 
copper parts. Basically, due to the high heat input, high 
thermal gradient, and high cooling rate during PBF-LB/M 
processing of CuCrZr alloys, these materials represent the 
microstructural features, including columnar grains aris-
ing from epitaxial growth and preferred orientation [4, 10]. 
Due to the high conductivity of copper alloys, the thermal 
gradient during their PBF-LB/M processing is higher than 
that of other metals, resulting in larger columnar grains. As 
a result, the PBF-LB/M-manufactured CuCrZr alloys have 
anisotropic mechanical and physical characteristics in dis-
tinct build directions [4]. Neglecting such important aniso-
tropic aspects, most prior investigations on the PBF-LB/M 
processing of CuCrZr alloys, unfortunately, concentrated on 
the influence of processing parameters on the microstruc-
ture and properties perpendicular to one single direction of 
the printed parts [4, 5, 12, 24–28]. The anisotropic micro-
structure of PBF-LB/M-produced CuCrZr alloys at the dif-
ferent build directions has also been shown in a few stud-
ies [10, 29, 30], but some complexities in the anisotropic 
microstructural features have also been reported due to the 
severe sensitivity of the PBF-LB/M process to the process 
parameters. For example, Hu et al. [11] observed that the 
crystallographic texture and the grain microstructure of their 
PBF-LB/M-manufactured Cu–Cr–Zr (Cr: 0.87 wt.% and Zr: 
0.12 wt.%) specimens for the horizontal and vertical planes 
all exhibit the same anisotropic trend, which is independ-
ent of the volumetric laser energy density and the defects 
in the specimen. In another study, Wang et al. [31] mod-
eled the heat transfer and melt-pool characteristics of PBF-
LB/M-produced CuCrZr (Cr: 0.88 wt.% and Zr: 0.14 wt.%) 
alloys and showed that the vertical and horizontal planes of 
the produced materials can have anisotropic microstructures 
of almost epigenetic grains growing parallel to the build-
ing direction (BD) and fine grains that are oriented 45° to 
the scanning direction (SD), respectively. Kulkarni et al. 
[32] also observed that their PBF-LB/M-produced CuCrZr 
(Cr: 0.99 wt.% and Zr: 0.06 wt.%) alloys have no crystal-
lographic texture but exhibit isotropic mechanical proper-
ties in such a way that the measured yield strength along 
the transverse orientation was 10–16% higher than that of 
the longitudinal orientation. Recently, Xie et al. [13] inves-
tigated the effect of build orientations on mechanical and 
thermal properties of PBF-LB/M-fabricated CuCrZr (Cr: 
0.50–0.70 wt.% and Zr: 0.06–0.15 wt.%) alloys and indi-
cated that the mechanical and thermal anisotropy attributes 
the stronger < 110 > grain orientation and a lower fraction

Furthermore, higher tensile strength in horizontal and angled

With respect to the reported state of the art, several 
research gaps are noted in this study. The literature indi-
cates that low fractions of keyhole or lack-of-fusion pores 
are typically present in PBF-LB/M-produced copper alloys, 
even when optimized parameters from the transition zone 
are used. However, the impact of these pores on the overall 
performance of the material has not been thoroughly inves-
tigated. In addition, most prior studies have overlooked the 
strong anisotropy in microstructure and properties across 
different build directions, often evaluating CuCrZr alloys in 
a single direction. Even the limited research exploring mul-
tiple directions has reported inconsistent and varied results 
regarding anisotropy. Furthermore, while process-induced 
pores are acknowledged as inherent to PBF-LB/M process-
ing, their specific role in influencing microstructural ani-
sotropy and directional variations in mechanical properties 
remains unexplored, leaving a critical gap in understanding 
their effects.
While lack-of-fusion or keyhole porosities frequency 
developed through PBF-LB/M processing of copper alloys, 
this study aims to evaluate the roles of such pores’ char-
acteristics on the anisotropic microstructure and mechani-
cal properties of the printed CuCrZr alloys. Therefore, the 
desired samples of this research were produced using the 
same CuCrZr-feedstock composition but process parameters 
from different parts of the PBF-LB/M processing window, 
near the conduction and keyhole regimes. The produced 
samples, which contain varied amounts of keyhole or lack-
of-fusion pores, were characterized in different planes ori-
ented to build direction. For the first time, the effect of the 
process-induced pores and their characteristics (e.g., size, 
shape, quantity, distribution, and orientation) are investi-
gated on the anisotropy of microstructure and mechanical 
properties of PBF-LB/M-produced alloys. Furthermore, 
this paper studied the mechanisms of keyholes or lack-of-
fusion pores evaluation during the melting and solidifica-
tion of melt pools and offers a comprehensive understanding 
of correlations between the development of various typed 
pores, microstructural characteristics (e.g., grains size and 
structure, preferred orientation, crystallographic texture, 
and anisotropy mechanism of microstructures) and aniso-
tropic mechanical behavior of PBF-LB/M-produced CuCrZr 
alloys.
2  Materials and method
CuCrZr powder (CCZ: 0.7 wt.% Cr, 0.07 wt.% Zr, 0.02 wt.% 
Si, 0.02 wt.% Fe, 0.02 wt.% other) with a mean particle 
size of 37 µm was supplied by Schmelzmetall Deutschland 
GmbH. Printing of bulk CuCrZr samples was performed 
utilizing the above-mentioned powder and an Aconity 
Mini PBF-LB/M machine (Aconity3D GmbH, Germany), 
equipped with a 500 W Nd-YAG laser that operates at a 
wavelength of 1070 nm. Figure 1 represents the programmed 
scanning pattern for printing different layers of CuCrZr sam-
ples on the stainless-steel substrates. Under an argon atmos-
phere, two kinds of CuCrZr samples (13 × 6 × 7 ­mm3) were 
produced utilizing two different laser powers (P) of 300 W 
and 380 W. For these experiments, the other printing param-
eters of scanning speed (s), hatch distance (h), and layer 
thickness (t) were set at 850 mm/s, 0.055 mm, and 0.025 
mm, respectively. The volumetric energy densities (VED) of 
the printing processes were then calculated using the equa-
tion P/(s·h·t) and came out to be 257 J/mm3 and 325 J/mm3.
The relative density of the produced alloys, as well as the 
characteristics of induced pores (amount, shape, size, and 
distribution) in each sample, were evaluated by XCT, Gen-
eral Electric v|tome|x L 300 machine. 2000 projections were 
acquired during each scan with an acquisition time of 2 s for 
each projection. The XCT measurements were performed on 
the cubic samples (2 × 4 × 8 ­mm3), with a tube voltage of 180 
kV, current of 60 μA, voxel size of 6 μm3, and by utilizing a 
0.5 mm Al filter. Data processing and visualization were per-
formed by using Fiji ImageJ method [37] and AvizoFire 9.4

To investigate the anisotropic microstructure and mechan-

longitudinal and transverse directions (parallel and per-

were prepared by grinding down to a grit size of 5 µm and 
mechanical polishing down to 1-µm grit size using diamond 
suspension. This was followed up by a chemo-mechanical 
polishing step using ­SiO2 polishing suspension (OPS and 
OPU, Struers, Willich, Germany). Finally, the electrolytic 
polishing and etching of the samples were carried out using 
a phosphoric acid-containing D2 electrolyte (Struers, Elec-
trolyte D2) under 24 V and for 20 s.
The mechanical properties of samples in both longitudi-
nal and transverse directions were also measured employ-
ing nanoindentation and compression test methods. The 
nanoindentation experiments were done utilizing a Bruker 
Hysitron TI 980 TriboIndenter at room temperature and 
until the indentation depth of 500 nm. Each experiment was 
repeated nine times at different positions on the samples’ 
surfaces. The compression tests were also performed using 
the machined cylindrical samples (D = 3 mm and H = 6 
mm) on a universal testing machine (Instron 4505, Instron, 
Darmstadt, Germany) at room temperature and a constant 
engineering strain rate of ­10−2 ­s−1. No lubricant was used 
for the measurements, and the displacement during the com-
pression test was measured with an HDM DD1 class 0.5

rams. Furthermore, two replicates were prepared from each 
longitudinal and transverse direction of the samples, and the 
values of compressive strength ­(Rp0.2) and slope of elastic 
deformation at lower stresses ­(ME) were calculated by the

3  Results
The transition zone for PBF-LB/M processing of the high-
est-density CuCrZr alloys is quite small, so dense sam-
ples can only be produced within a restricted PBF-LB/M 
process window of optimal manufacturing parameters 
(P = 300–380 W, s = 850 mm/s, h = 0.055 mm, t = 0.025 
mm, and VED = 257–325 J/mm3). Although the samples 
produced in this zone have the highest density conceivable, 
they still retain certain pores (such as keyholes and lack-
of-fusion) in their structure [19, 20, 22, 23]. In the prelimi-
nary phase of this research, several samples were produced 
using a similar CuCrZr alloy powder and with different 
PBF-LB/M processing parameters. It has been concluded 
that the transition zone for PBF-LB/M processing of 
CuCrZr alloys lies between 300-W and 380W laser power, 
so conduction and keyhole zones appear below 300-W 
and above 380W laser powers, respectively. Furthermore, 
still small amount of lack-of-fusion and keyhole pores are 
observed in the structure of samples produced with laser 
powers between 300 and 380W. To examine the impact of 
defects on microstructural and mechanical property anisot-
ropy, two CuCrZr samples were produced using identical 
alloy powder and consistent processing conditions, with 
laser powers of 300 W and 380 W to represent the lack-of-
fusion and keyhole regimes, respectively. PBF-LB/M pro-
cessing of CuCrZr alloys with these parameters has been 
accompanied by the emergence of varied shapes and sizes 
of pores within the samples. The distribution of such pores 
in the produced samples has been analyzed by the XCT 
method. As seen in Fig. 2, the sample produced with the 
lower laser power (300 W) contains plenty of pores with 
varying shapes and sizes. Based on the quantitative XCT 
results, the relative density of this sample is 98.883%. The 
corresponding size distribution histogram demonstrates 
that the pores formed in this sample come in a broad range 
of sizes and shapes, including two different types of small 
(< 50 µm) and large (50–300 µm) pores. Furthermore, it 
can be seen in the aspect ratio (length to thickness ratio) 
histogram that the detected pores have also wide distribu-
tions in such a way that contain both semi-spherical and 
elongated pores. According to the XCT 3D images and 2D 
graphs taken from different directions of this sample, the 
small pores are almost spherical and randomly dispersed 
throughout the printed alloy. However, the larger pores 
have an elongated shape and are arranged parallel to each 
other and perpendicular to BD. These elongated pores 
have nearly consistent spacing comparable with the thick-
ness of printed layers and imply that the pores were devel-
oped in the interlayers’ spaces. The presence of elongated 
and parallelly arranged pores between the printed layers 
suggests that the lack-of-fusion phenomenon occurred 
during the production of this sample. On the other side, 
CuCrZr alloy produced with the higher laser power (380 
W) has very low porosity values, and its relative density 
was measured at 99.991%. Based on the XCT images and 
measured size distribution frequencies, the pores in this 
sample are randomly dispersed and have a narrow size 
distribution (average pore length of 40 µm). Moreover, 
the related aspect ratio histogram indicates that such small 
pores have almost irregular semi-spherical shapes. These 
pores can be related to the formation of keyholes, which

It should also be noted that the smaller spherical pores in 
both samples may also have a metallurgical basis. For exam-
ple, capillary pores can be formed due to the domination of 
capillarity and tension forces on gravity and the entrapment 
of liquid metal within the interstitial spaces between powder 
particles [38]. However, these small capillaries (up to 15 
µm) are below the XCT detection level and were not quanti-
fied for any of the samples. The gas pores which are formed 
by the entrapment of gas within the molten pool, and pit 
cavities which are the result of the stacking of multiple pores 
[39] can also have a quasi-spherical shape and randomly dis-
tribute in both PBF-LB/M-produced samples. Despite their 
apparent similarity to keyholes, these metallurgical pores 
can be distinguished by their sizes and shapes. Depending 
on the dynamics of the molten pool and the conditions of 
collapse, keyhole pores are usually elongated, irregular, or 
spherical. They are also larger than metallurgical pores, 
with sizes ranging from a few micrometers to hundreds of 
micrometers. Conversely, depending on the gas composition 
and processing parameters, gas pores can range from sub-
micron to a few tens of micrometers and are often spherical 
because of the molten metal’s surface tension. Pit cavities 
which are smaller than keyholes have mostly elongated or 
irregular shapes [19, 38].
Figure 3 depicts SEM pictures of various planes of the 
produced samples. Fine equiaxed grains of 10–50 µm diam-
eter are seen in the cross-sectional microstructure of both 
samples perpendicular to BD (transverse planes). However, 
distinct microstructures from the transverse plane can be 
observed in the cross sections parallel to BD (longitudinal 
planes), indicating microstructural anisotropy in different 
directions of the samples. Indeed, the microstructure of the 
longitudinal planes includes large and elongated columnar 
grains that are mostly stretched parallel to BD and in the 
direction of the solidification front. The grain size in the 
300-W sample was restricted (up to ≈120 µm) and occurred 
at an angle of ± 30° to the BD. In this case, the presence of 
lack-of-fusion pores can cause columnar grain segmenta-
tion across the layers, so smaller grains and varied growth 
directions have been discovered around the lack-of-fusion 
pores. The 380-W sample, on the other hand, exhibits a much 
longer grain size (average grain length of ≈250 µm). These 
grains were grown perfectly parallel to BD, and keyhole 
pores were generally found inside the grains.

It should be noted that the precipitation hardening heat 
treatment has not been performed on the printed samples. 
The precipitation hardening is a process for enhancing the 
material’s strength and hardness through three heat treat-
ment steps annealing (heating to 980–1000 °C to dissolve 
Cr and Zr into the copper matrix and form a supersaturated 
solid solution), aging (heating to 450–550 °C to precipi-
tate fine Cr and Zr particles), and cooling naturally to room 
temperature to retains the precipitated structure within the 
copper matrix. Furthermore, the fast-cooling steps of PBF-
LB/M processing do not result in the precipitate production 
[4, 40]. Regarding, no precipitates were detected by the EDS 
elemental mapping analyses, instead uniform distribution of 
Cr suggests that Cr (and Zr) completely dissolved in the Cu 
matrix. The EDS analyses also indicate that oxidation may 
happen within the pores and be accompanied by the genera-
tion of Cr oxidization products.

4  Discussion
During the PBF-LB/M process, laser irradiation to the 
powder feedstock and its subsequent absorption and con-
duction to the depth of the layer raises the temperature 
of the powders to a temperature higher than their melting 
point and causes the powder to melt in a parabola-shaped 
melt pool [41]. Assuming a constant absorption coefficient 
across all feedstock contents and constant scanning param-
eters throughout the printing process, the dimensions of 
these melt pools remain identical across all weld tracks. As 
observed in Fig. 1, the scanning patterns used for creating 
these weld tracks rotate their SD by 90° in each layer while 
utilizing a hatch spacing of 55 µm. Since the appropriate 
hatch spacing values were chosen for scanning purposes, 
the applied weld tracks overlap partially, and their width is 
nearly comparable to the applied hatch spacing value. How-
ever, the depth of these melt pools (D) depends greatly on 
the applied laser energy; therefore, different melting modes 
may be achieved in the weld tracks by varying the laser 
power. The effect of laser power on the shape of the melt 
pools, melting modes, defect formation, grain orientation, 
and development of anisotropic microstructure are schemati-
cally shown in Fig. 7.
Since copper has a low laser absorption coefficient, its 
PBF-LB/M printing requires higher laser powers than those 
of other metals such as Fe and Ni (absorbance of Nd:YAG 
laser by Cu, Ni, and Fe were reported around 2%, 26%, and 
38%, respectively [42]). If lower laser powers are utilized 
to produce these parts, copper particles absorb just a small 
portion of the laser’s energy, and a limited amount of energy 
will be provided to melt the copper particles. As a result, the 
generated melt pool would have a limited depth, so the cop-
per powder in the lower part of the applied layer may not be

in which the aspect ratio of the melt pool, the ratio of the 
melt-pool depth to half its width, is less than 0.5 [17]. As 
shown in Fig. 7, the emergence of lack-of-fusion defects in 
the sample will also be accelerated if the depth of the applied 
melt pool is less than or equal to the thickness of the printed 
layer (t). On the other side, increasing the laser power and 
heat energy absorbed by the particles not only raises the tem-

as the depth of heat penetration into the preceding layers. If 
the laser power and depth of the melt pool increase in such 
a way that the aspect ratio of the melt pool exceeds 0.5 and 
1.1, the transition and conduction modes will be responsible 
for explaining the melt-pool formation mechanisms [23].
Similar effects of laser power on the geometry and dimen-
sion of the melt pools have been reported for PBF-LB/M 
processing of other metals. For the use case of Ti-6Al-4V 
alloy, as an example, increasing the laser power from 100 to 
200 W can increase the melt-pool depth from approximately 
50 μm to 100 μm and the width from 150 μm to 300 μm, 
depending on the material and specific process parameters 
[43]. Furthermore, several analytical methodologies were 
developed for modeling the PBF-LB/M melt-pool dimen-
sions for both the conduction and keyhole regimes as a func-
tion of laser power [18, 43–46]. Computational simulation 
of the melt-pool dynamics during PBF-LB/M processing 
of Inconel 718 shows that increasing the laser powers gen-
erally leads to a larger and deeper melt pool and changes 
the melting mode from conduction to keyhole mode [44]. 
Another numerical simulation has also indicated that as 
the laser power increases, the depth of depression caused 
by the recoil pressure increases, and the molten-pool depth 
increases accordingly [45]. Furthermore, mapping the PBF-
LB/M processing defects boundaries of Ti-6Al-4V alloy has 
shown that large-scale keyhole defects were located in the 
characteristic high-power regions of the processing win-
dow, where the ratio of melt-pool width to spot size can 
equivalently be used to establish the transition to keyholing 
with processing parameter changes [18]. Considering the

As shown in Fig. 7, when a deeper melt pool is created 
by the keyhole mechanism, the pool walls play a significant 
role in the internal reflection of the laser, increasing laser 
absorption by the melt pool and its penetration into the melt 
pool. In this case, it has been reported that the bottom half of 
the keyhole absorbs four times more laser energy compared 
to its upper half [47, 48]. Since the melted copper alloy has 
a much higher absorption than its solid powder [19], the 
high absorption of the laser and accumulation of excessive 
energy input at the scan tracks cause the vaporization of the 
melted metal and the formation of vapor bubbles. Although 
the capillary pressures caused by surface tension try to close 
these bubbles, there will not be enough time for the key-
hole to be closed or filled with melted metal due to the high 
thermal conductivity of copper and the rapid dissipation of 
the absorbed heat [2, 20]. Therefore, the vapor bubbles are 
mostly trapped during the solidification process and result 
in the formation of keyhole-induced porosity in the 380-W 
sample. Furthermore, the excessive energy input of the laser 
beam or heat accumulation at the scan track will intensify 
the temperature gradients at the melt pool and cause the 
liquid metal to flow from areas of low surface tension to 
areas of high surface tension. This phenomenon, known as 
the Marangoni flow of melt metal, can also promote pool 
instability, resulting in further cavity entrapment and key-
hole development [19]. Because the depth of the melt pool 
in the keyhole mode can extend to multiple printed layers 
and induce their partial remelting, the keyhole porosities can 
also be eliminated or joined together as a result of the layers 
remelting. The keyhole-induced pores are typically 20–100 
µm in length and distributed randomly across the 380 W 
sample. It should be noted that these pores are different from 
those smaller metallurgical holes that may likewise spread 
homogeneously in the printed materials. Such holes, which 
can be detected in both 300 W and 380 W samples, have 
mostly the metallurgical origins like gas holes or pit cavities.
While the powder melting and modes of melt-pool forma-
tion determine the porosity development in the PBF-LB/M-
produced sample, the solidification of such melt pools along 
with the induced porosities control the microstructure of the 
printed samples. Figure 7 schematically depicts the mecha-
nism of melt-pool solidification, as well as the nucleation 
and development of grains in its up (transverse) and lat-
eral (longitudinal) directions. The solidification front in the 
transverse planes extends from the wall of the preceding 
weld tracks to the center of the melt pool. Here, the rapid 
cooling at the edges of the melt pool, where it interacts with 
the solidified material of preceding tracks and faces with 
high thermal gradients, induces multiple nucleation sites 
and promotes nucleation of equiaxed grains. Such nucle-
ated grains cannot grow substantially throughout the width 
of the weld track due to the rapid cooling, overlapping, and 
re-melting of successive layers, instead partially grow until 
the weld track center or adjunct grains. As a result, differ-
ent grains nucleate on the surface of the weld track during 
the rapid solidification of the melt pool, but their growth 
in the transverse direction is restricted to the width of the 
weld track. Accordingly, the solidification of the melt pool 
in the transverse direction is accompanied by the achieve-
ment of fine equiaxed microstructures (Fig. 3). However, 
the solidification front in the longitudinal direction extends 
from the bottom to the top of the melt pool and is parallel 
to BD. Because the grains in each new layer may simply 
nucleate on the grains of the preceding layer, the new grains 
inherit the orientation of the preceding layer and cause epi-
taxial growth of long columnar grains along the BD and over 
multiple succeeding layers. The epitaxial growth of long 
columnar grains across several layers is therefore accompa-
nied by their strong crystallographic orientation. Although 
the preferred epitaxial growth direction of the FCC crys-
tals is < 100 > , the PBF-LB/M-produced CuCrZr alloys 
showed intense < 101 > textures parallel to BD. A simi-
lar < 101 > texture was also reported in several PBF-LB/M-
manufactured copper alloys; however, the texture intensity 
was only up to ≈6 [4, 6, 8, 13]. Moreover, the 90° rotation 
of SD in each layer did not affect texture since it resulted 
in the same crystallographic orientations. Here, it seems 
that the applied high laser powers affected the shape of the 
melt pool and changed the curvature of the weld tracks in 
the < 101 > direction [31]. Since the grains tend to grow per-
pendicular to the weld track’s curvature and in the direction 
of heat transfer, their growth has thus been directed primar-
ily in the < 101 > direction. Therefore, the development of 
fine equiaxed grains in the transverse planes and elongated 
columnar grains in the longitudinal planes of the printed 
samples results in their high microstructural anisotropy as 
has also been found for some PBF-LB/M-produced CuCrZr 
alloys [10, 29, 30].
However, as seen in Figs. 3, 4, 5, laser power varia-
tions and the emergence of structural defects arising from 
lack-of-fusion and keyhole modes may have a significant 
impact on the microstructural anisotropy of printed materi-
als. When lack-of-fusion pores are induced into the 300 W 
sample, the longitudinal microstructure is developed by the 
limited-length columnar grains of weak orientation along 
BD (Fig. 5). The applied laser energy is too low in this case 
to provide the high-temperature melt pool and enable partial 
melting or heating the of the preceding layers. Therefore, a 
strong temperature gradient is generated from the top of the 
melt pool to its interface with the cooler preceding layer. 
Based on the analytical Rosenthal model [49], copper alloys

possess a high solidification rate owing to their high heat-
transfer coefficients, the aforementioned intense tempera-
ture gradients, as well as the high scanning speeds utilized, 
considerably increased the solidification rate of the 300-W 
sample. Such rapid solidification restricts the diffusion and 
growth of the grains and promotes the development of fine 
microstructures. Furthermore, the presence of elongated 
lack-of-fusion pores at the layers’ interfaces prevents the 
epitaxial growth of new grains on these of the preceding 
layers, which limits the growth of columnar grains and leads 
to the formation of equiaxed grains at the interruption of 
interfacial pores. Indeed, limited remelting of the preceding 
layer and the weak layers’ interfaces encourage the solidi-
fying metals to heterogeneously nucleate on the preceding 
layer instead of growing epitaxially on their former grains. 
The grain growth may therefore be limited to specific lay-
ers. Even though all these new grains develop parallel to 
BD, they suffer minor angular changes in crystallographic 
grain orientation due to differences in heat-gradient direc-
tions. Consequently, the developed microstructures exhibit 
a weaker texture orientation along BD as well as significant 
intergranular misorientation (color gradient) in their grain 
structure (Fig. 5).
In the 380 W sample, keyhole mode melting with high 
energy input raises the melt-pool temperature and causes 
remelting of underlying layers. This increases the melt-
pool depth across multiple layers, establishing a controlled 
temperature gradient and solidification rate along the melt 
pool. As a result, grains grow epitaxially on those in the 
preceding layers, maintaining their orientation and forming 
long columnar grains. Small keyhole pores within the grains 
have negligible impact on nucleation or growth orientation. 
Additionally, the increased laser power deepens the melt 
pool and accentuates its curvature in the < 101 > direction, 
driving grains to grow perpendicular to this orientation. 
Consequently, long columnar grains aligned perpendicular 
to < 101 > form, leading to pronounced microstructural ani-
sotropy in the 380 W alloy (Fig. 4).
The microstructural anisotropy observed in the trans-
verse and longitudinal directions of the PBF-LB/M-pro-
duced CuCrZr alloys has also resulted in their mechanical 
properties anisotropy. According to the findings of Table 1, 
the compression properties of both samples are higher in 
the transverse direction than in the longitudinal one. The 
textural orientation of columnar grains relative to the force 
application axes can explain this outcome. In the transverse 
samples, the loading axis is perpendicular to the columnar 
grains, and therefore a strong force is required to deform 
the columnar grains. Compared to transverse samples, the 
loading axis in longitudinal samples is parallel to the col-
umn grains, hence, plastic deformation is easier to compress 
columnar grains, and a smaller amount of force may over-
come the frictional force between the grains to deflect them. 
In other words, the deformation axis in transverse samples 
is aligned with the smaller dimensions of the grains and 
hence perpendicular to a significantly higher number of 
grain boundaries. The grain boundaries act as barriers to 
dislocation motion, so the material deforms when the stress 
concentration at the grain boundaries is high enough to over-
come such dislocation pile-ups and cause the slip to propa-
gate between grains. As a result, finer grains have a greater 
grain boundary and dislocation density, which impedes dis-
location motion and thereby strengthens the material [50]. 
The higher compressive strength of the produced samples 
in the transverse directions can also be related to their crys-
tallographic textures and the Taylor factor variation. While 
the Taylor factor evaluates the favorable slip systems for 
plastic deformation of polycrystalline materials at different 
crystallographic grain orientations, those directions of the 
samples that contain the grain orientations with higher Tay-
lor factors require more stress for plastic deformation [51, 
52]. In the case of FCC crystals, the Taylor factor is mini-
mum for the < 100 > crystallographic texture and increases 
in the < 101 > crystallographic texture [51, 52]. Therefore, 
the < 101 > textures of the transverse samples along the load-
ing direction may cause its higher compressive strength than 
that of longitudinal samples with dominant < 100 > -ori-
ented grains. Microstructure anisotropy in different sample 
directions significantly impacts the material’s performance 
in applications requiring isotropic properties by creating 
directional mechanical properties variations. In other words, 
due to the mentioned microstructure anisotropy, the trans-
verse directions of the samples provide higher compressive 
strengths. In applications requiring isotropic properties, this 
results in uneven load distribution, where the material may 
fail prematurely in weaker longitudinal directions. In addi-
tionally, the disparity in strength can lead to stress concen-
tration zones, reducing the material’s overall reliability and 
limiting its use in components exposed to uniform forces, 
such as pressure vessels or structural frameworks.
Eventually, it should be noted that due to the rapid solidi-
fication of PBF-LB/M processed samples and lack of pre-
cipitation hardening heat treatment processes, precipitates 
were not considerably detected in the samples. However, in 
the case of precipitation hardening, the created precipitates 
can pin grain boundaries and restrict the grain growth dur-
ing the solidification process, so their distribution, size, and 
morphology may affect the anisotropic microstructure and 
mechanical properties of the CuCrZr alloys. With regard to 
the microstructural evaluations, precipitation hardening of 
CuCrZr alloys will cause precipitation of fine Cr-rich par-
ticles within the copper matrix, which can pin dislocations 
and refine the grain structure, such an event may respec-
tively affect the microstructural anisotropy. However, the 
precipitation hardening treatment is expected to more affect 
the materials’ properties. While the electrical and thermal

and hardness improved because of dispersion strengthening, 
grain boundary strengthening (hall–Petch effect), and dislo-
cation pinning (Orowan mechanism) [6, 8, 25]. Especially, 
the micromechanical properties variations (e.g., nanoin-

mostly be affected by the precipitation hardening treatment.
Keyhole pores, with their low concentrations, small 
sizes, semi-spherical shapes, and uniform distribution, have 
minimal impact on mechanical anisotropy, whereas lack-of-
fusion pores, characterized by high concentrations, larger 
sizes, and elongated shapes, significantly contribute to it. 
The large and elongated lack-of-fusion pores (up to 300-μm 
long) typically form along the interfaces between powder 
layers and are oriented perpendicular to the build direction 
(BD). Especially, this orientation causes significant anisot-
ropy in the mechanical properties of PBF-LB/M-produced 
alloys. As illustrated in Fig. 7, the lack-of-fusion pores in 
longitudinal samples are oriented perpendicular to the axis 
of force application. This alignment results in a pronounced 
reduction in the strengthening effect typically provided by 
grain boundaries. The presence of these elongated pores cre-
ates weak planes that are less able to resist applied loads, 
leading to simplified crack propagation paths. In other 
words, the unbonded locations thrive as stress concentra-
tor zones and limit the ability of the material to withstand 
applied loads. The arrangement of elongated lack-of-fusion 
porosities parallel to each other also interrupts the conti-
nuity of the material, reduces the materials’ ductility, and 
makes them more prone to brittle failure. Consequently, 
under compressive stresses the material experiences more 
fracture initiation sites, straightforward crack formation, and 
reduced elongation until fracture. This contributes to the 
300-W sample’s lower compressive strength in the longitu-
dinal direction. Indeed, the 300-W sample which contains a 
high amount of elongated lack-of-fusion pores exhibits lower 
microstructural anisotropy but higher mechanical property 
anisotropy than the 380 W sample.
The 380-W sample shows overall higher mechanical 
properties in both transverse and longitudinal directions. In 
this case, keyhole porosities can act as stress concentration 
areas for crack initiation, leading to reduced strength and 
lower ability of the produced samples to deform plastically 
before failure. However, such small pores are mostly closed 
under compressive stresses, making the materials’ deforma-
tion more uniform. Here, the keyhole pores caused a lower 
level of mechanical properties anisotropy in transverse and 
longitudinal directions. Furthermore, the impacts of porosi-
ties and mechanical property anisotropy are not apparent in 
the nanoindentation test, which was done on a much smaller 
scale of the sample and probably inside the single grains. 
The higher hardness of the 380-W sample, on the other hand, 
can be explained by factors such as the crystallographic ori-
entation of grains, enhanced intergranular misorientation, 
probable precipitation hardening, or changes in the alloy 
chemical composition throughout the 380 W PBF-LB/M 
process [53].
5  Conclusion
The narrow transition zone for PBF-LB/M manufacturing of 
copper components has a high overlap with the conduction 
and keyhole zones, so even within the optimized process 
window, PBF-LB/M processing of copper and its alloys 
is accompanied by the formation of minor defects such as 
keyhole and lack-of-fusion pores. The findings of this study 
suggest that finding more narrow transition zones and even 
its shift to the keyhole zone can prevent from development 
of elongated lack-of-fusion pores and significantly reduce 
porosity concentration within the printed samples.
When an increase in the laser energy shifts the processing 
modes to the keyhole side, the higher heat energy absorbed 
increases the melt-pool depth, so that both internal reflection 
of the laser by the pool walls and higher laser absorption of 
the molten copper led to heat accumulation, melt vaporiza-
tion, and consequently the formation of vapor bubbles. As 
a result of trapping these bubbles during the solidification 
process, semi-spherical and small (≈40 µm) keyhole pores 
are formed in random regions of the sample. Due to the high 
thermal gradient over the melt pool and their rapid solidifi-
cation, the keyhole pores cannot prevent the epitaxial growth 
of long columnar grains over multiple succeeding layers. 
Therefore, the growth of long columnar grains (average 
length of ≈250 µm) with strong < 101 > orientation (texture 
intensity of 21) along the BD resulted in the strong micro-
structural anisotropy of this sample.
In contrast, close to the conduction zone, the input energy 
is not high enough to penetrate through the powder layer and 
cause complete melting of the lower powders, remelting of 
the preceding layer, and fusion of partially melted powder 
to the underlying layer. Therefore, elongated lack-of-fusion 
pores (up to 300-µm long) are formed at the layers’ inter-
faces. Indeed, such defects are oriented parallel to each other 
and perpendicular to the solidification front, which highly 
hinders the columnar growth of the grains. Instead of epi-
taxial grain growth, there is here more tendency for hetero-
geneous nucleation of new grains on the preceding layers. 
Both the limited growth of columnar grains (up to ≈120 
µm) and the formation of equiaxed grains at the interruption 
of interfacial lack-of-fusion pores eventually resulted in the 
weaker texture orientation of the produced alloy (texture 
intensity of 7.3).
Due to the textural orientation of columnar grains rela-
tive to the force application axes, both samples represented

Abstract: Due to the high reflectance and heat conductivity of copper and its alloys, the processing window for laser-based powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) processing of high-density copper components fundamentally overlaps with conduction and keyhole melting zones, resulting in the emergence of certain pores in the structure of printed parts. The present research aims to study how the development of process-induced lack-of-fusion or keyhole porosities during the PBF-LB/M process can affect the anisotropic microstructure and mechanical properties of the produced copper alloys. For this purpose, several samples were produced utilizing a similar CuCrZr-feedstock composition but varied process parameters from different areas of the PBF- LB/M processing window, specifically at laser powers of 300 W and 380 W which define the boarders of the conduction and keyhole regimes. X-ray computed tomography (XCT) revealed that the 300-W and 380-W samples achieved relative densities of 98.88% and 99.99%, respectively, with elongated lack-of-fusion pores forming at 300 W and semi-spherical keyhole pores at 380 W. Microstructural analyses employing scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) demonstrated strong anisotropy in different build directions of the samples, owing to the growth of long columnar grains with intense < 101 > orientation along the build directions. Here, the emergence of different types of pores can cause competition between the epitaxial growth of columnar grains and the heterogeneous nucleation of new grains on the layers’ interfaces, thereby significantly varying the grain size, preferred orientation, crystallographic texture, and microstructural anisotropy of the samples. Furthermore, compression tests and nanoindentation measurements of the printed alloys in the longitudinal and transverse directions revealed that the 300 W and 380 W samples exhibited compressive strength anisotropies of 0.061 and 0.072, and average nanoindentation hardness values of 1.3 GPa and 1.5 GPa, respectively. The orientation of elongated lack-of-fusion porosities perpendicular to the loading axis was identified as the most damaging factor, significantly reducing mechanical performance compared to the uniformly distributed keyhole pores.
